blocks.text: This section presents the capstone’s main practical output: a sequence of diagnostic questions and stage-by-stage guidance drawn from the cases, so founders can test financing decisions against the evidence and investors can test whether their capital suits the business. It is a decision aid, not a prescription: each recommendation depends on the conditions noted alongside it, and an instrument that suits a business in principle may be unavailable or uneconomic in a given market.

items.title: What is being financed?
items.text: Platform capabilities and operating expenses, or an identifiable asset or receivable such as a loan book, devices, payment float, inventory or vehicles? Usually only the latter can support debt.

items.title: Who is best placed to own and operate the asset?
items.text: The company, a partner that already owns it (car owners, logistics firms), or a lender that can hold it more cheaply?

items.title: Who should bear the risks?
items.text: Credit, commercial, currency, operational, insurance and asset-loss risks can sit with different parties; each allocation should be written into contracts and enforced.

items.title: What instrument fits?
items.text: Weigh cash-flow predictability and seasonality, asset life, utilisation and residual value, repayment duration, debt-service capacity and the consequences of a missed payment, interest cost, collateral, guarantees and covenants, and the currency of revenues against that of liabilities.

items.title: What conditions must hold first?
items.text: A repayment record lenders can underwrite; lenders willing to lend in the right currency, at a price and tenor the asset can bear; and a regulatory route, such as a lending or banking licence or approval to securitise.

items.title: What happens if a relationship changes?
items.text: Test the structure against the loss of a lender, a dominant customer or platform, or a risk-carrying partner, and against a devaluation or a round that fails to close. Weigh, too, the margin and control given up to any partner that finances or operates the asset.

figure.caption: The six diagnostic questions, asked in order before sizing a raise. Source: Section 07.

blocks.title: Step 2: Decide who carries the asset and its risks

blocks.text: Before deciding how much to raise, founders should split the capital need in two. Platform capital funds technology, people, licences and market entry, carries venture risk and suits equity. Asset capital funds loan books, devices, float, inventory, vehicles and warehouses. For each asset, the founder chooses among broad routes, which in practice are often combined:

blocks.html:
Route
When it fits
Evidence
Condition
Leave it with a partner
Before the company has the data to price the asset’s risk, or where a partner can own or finance the asset more cheaply
Autogirl, Feegor, Earthbond
Enforce the risk transfer in contracts (insurance, guarantors, escrow, title); accept the partner’s share of margin and control; avoid dependence on one partner
Own it and fund it with debt
Once repayment or utilisation data supports a lender’s credit decision and cash flows are predictable enough to service debt
M-KOPA, MNT-Halan, Omnibiz; NALA (payment float)
Diversify lenders and repayment channels; match debt currency and tenor to the asset; size debt to downside cash flows and covenants (Moove shows the cost of a single repayment channel)
Fund it from deposits under a banking licence
Where the company can obtain a deposit-taking licence and meet its capital requirements
Moniepoint
Accept supervision and capital requirements; deposits fund lending only within prudential limits
Own it and fund it with equity
For small or short-lived needs with no suitable lender, or where cash flows are too uncertain to service debt
Sendy (cautionary)
Equity is usually the most expensive capital for an asset; keep the exposure small and time-limited

blocks.text: One test determines which route a structure follows: who holds title to the asset, and who carries the return risk. In Autogirl’s Prado offer, shares would make it equity; investor-owned, Autogirl-managed vehicles would make it off-balance-sheet asset capital; a guaranteed return would make it debt in substance, whatever the label. The same test separates NALA’s corridor facility (a working-capital line against payment flows, not a loan book) from lending, and will decide how LemFi’s credit products should be financed, depending on whether LemFi or its lending partner carries the loans.

blocks.html:
Shares→ equity
Investor-owned, company-managed assets→ off-balance-sheet asset capital
A guaranteed return→ debt in substance, whatever the label

blocks.text: The stage bands below are indicative. Revenue thresholds are rough markers; a company’s lender access, regulatory status and track record matter more than its revenue band.

blocks.html:
DimensionEarlypre-$1M ARRGrowth$1–10M ARRScale$10M+ ARR
TimingRaise to validate, not to scale. Pivot before institutionalising (NALA).Raise from strength, after proof of unit economics or profitability where possible. Do not size costs to an unraised round (Sendy).Raise counter-cyclically where the structure allows it (MNT-Halan, M-KOPA in 2023).
InstrumentRevenue, grants, prizes and accelerator money layered for minimal dilution (Autogirl, Feegor, Earthbond).Equity for the platform; receivables, asset-finance or working-capital facilities for the book or float once lenders will price it (NALA’s 2026 facility).Debt at scale: securitisation, syndicated and sustainability-linked facilities. Equity for M&A and new markets.
Asset routePartners carry vehicles, stock and credit.Bring assets onto the balance sheet, funded with debt, once data supports pricing and lenders are available (Omnibiz); otherwise stay with partners.Own the book where it is cheaper than partner funding; diversify funding sources, currencies and repayment channels.
Investor selectionInvestors and sponsors who become partners (Wema Bank for Feegor). Identify the lead for the first priced round before grants run out.Lead investors based in the customer’s market (Highland Europe for LemFi); DFIs as lenders where their mandate is strongest (M-KOPA).Domestic institutions ahead of a local listing (MNT-Halan); strategic buyers ahead of a trade sale.
DilutionKeep the cap table small enough to allow a pivot.Protect ownership through instrument choice, not only through valuation.Measure dilution against assets financed, not equity raised.
Decline / delayDelay institutional capital until the model is proven, and be able to show investors the delay is a choice.Decline capital that funds expansion before one market is profitable.Decline capital whose return expectations conflict with the likely exit.
Dependency riskMap every partner the model relies on for supply, credit or demand.Avoid repayments that depend on a single outside platform (Moove).Diversify lenders, partners and markets so no single exit or failure halts the business.
CurrencyKeep costs and liabilities in the currency of revenue; avoid dollar liabilities against local-currency income.Borrow in the asset’s currency where local lenders exist; price hedging into any dollar facility.Use local debt markets and listings where available (MNT-Halan).
LiquidityState the likely exit early (Autogirl: trade sale).Build an investor base whose return expectations fit that exit.Plan the listing or secondary route; a domestic exchange works for local-asset businesses (MNT-Halan).
